name: Rows that match columns
brief:
`grid` is a square table of sensor readings with `n` rows and `n` columns. Row `r` matches column `c` when they hold the same readings in the same order: `grid[r][k] == grid[k][c]` for every `k`. Return the number of pairs `(r, c)` that match.

Write `count_row_column_matches(grid)`.

Example. In `[[1, 2], [2, 1]]` row 0 reads 1, 2 and so does column 0. Row 1 reads 2, 1 and so does column 1. No other pair matches, so the answer is 2.
constraints: $0 \le n \le 300$, each reading a whole number between $-10^9$ and $10^9$.
$O(n^2)$ time is the target. Comparing every row with every column cell by cell takes $O(n^3)$.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Count each row as a tuple in a dict. Then read each column as a tuple and add how many rows equal it.

examples.note: Row 0 matches column 0 and row 1 matches column 1.
Every row and every column reads 1, 1, so all four pairs match.

tests.call: count_row_column_matches([[(i + j) % 7 for j in range(300)] for i in range(300)])
count_row_column_matches([[(i * j) % 3 for j in range(300)] for i in range(300)])

how: Submit runs 12 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: A row as a tuple is a dict key, and each column is looked up against the row counts.
Equal rows repeat, so a set of rows counts each match once and undercounts.
Building the tuples reads each cell twice, so the work is $O(n^2)$.

planted.slip: It intersects sets, so a row or column that repeats is counted once instead of once per pair.
It sorts each row and column, so the same readings in another order count as a match.

planted.code:
def count_row_column_matches(grid):
    return sum(1 for i, col in enumerate(zip(*grid)) if tuple(grid[i]) == col)
planted.slip: It compares row `i` only with column `i`, so it misses matches off the diagonal.
Gluing the readings into one string merges `(1, 11)` with `(11, 1)`.
